rv.q: But this is just a brilliantly conceived and executed piece, and I hope it yields Crystal another Tony Award.
Crystal is too much the entertainer to leave the stage without some light and hope.
With “860,” he proves that he has only grown more skilled at deploying laughter to assuage the pain of grief.
Against all odds, Crystal is again bringing a lot of that to Broadway.
He is a model mensch, kind in his outlook and quick to share credit with others...
It's tough to muster much to complain about this production, however slight it might end up feeling.
If, like me, you are a fan, you will find much to enjoy in director Scott Ellis’ classy but strikingly intimate production.
But all that warm, crowd-pleasing material is incongruously, fascinatingly, and not so comfortably fitted inside a story about great loss.
860 is a wonderful gift to audiences in need of a reason to celebrate life in all its wild incarnations – the good, the bad and even the ugly.
860 is as succinct as it is poignant, with Crystal taking audience members by the hand and down his memory lane — and refusing to let go of their hearts.
It’s a remarkable piece of storytelling, one that finds Crystal at his most vulnerable without ever sacrificing the impeccable comic timing that made him a household name.

It is Billy Crystal at his very best, aided by Scott Ellis, who directs the evening, and also supported by Crystal's frequent collaborator, the composer and lyricist Marc Shaiman, who has provided original music and adaptations of well-known songs that accompany the performance.
We are offered only a glimpse of Irwin’s brilliance as a clown and the prescription of laughter is not adequate.
This is both the funniest and saddest show on Broadway right now, and with good reason.
The beauty of his performance (as well as Scott Ellis’s direction) is the buoyancy it maintains throughout.
Billy Crystal's 860 is a funny and touching reminder that there's truly no place like home.
860 is a master class in the autobiographical blending of humor and emotion.

But even if Crystal didn’t want to take that path, there remains (for me) a slightly uncomfortable fit between the dramatic tale of what happened to 860 (the house) and the far funnier stories that make up the rest of Crystal’s personal and professional life.
Crystal leaps head first into that Palisades fire.
I could have easily and happily stayed longer listening to him tell more stories and jokes.
Sometimes, seriously, all you can do is laugh.
Still, there is a reason Crystal became a celebrity; he is good at what he does; a practiced storyteller, a funny man.
Tender without sappiness, sarcastic without cynicism, and profoundly human, 860 is not to be missed.
Otherwise, this is one of the most heartfelt and moving solo shows in recent memory.
By the end of 860, you'll be tempted to offer him a warm hug instead of a standing ovation.
Those unfamiliar with Crystal's work should make a date at the Imperial Theatre.
Very few start from real loss and come out the other side generous and funny.
If you make anything drawn from your own life, 860 is a masterclass in turning private loss into something an audience can hold.
We are offered only a glimpse of Irwin's brilliance as a clown and the prescription of laughter is not adequate.

cn.t: Critics praise Billy Crystal's heartfelt and hilarious one-man show, which transforms the devastating loss of his longtime home in the 2025 Palisades Fire into a moving celebration of family, memory, and the healing power of laughter.

sg.ra: Closest and most direct view of the stage at Imperial Theatre, with the fullest sound. The standard top pick for any show here.
An elevated, full-stage view with no orchestra-level neck-craning — especially strong for shows with big staging or choreography.
A modest side angle on the stage but still close and clear — a reliable choice when center seats are sold out.
Farther from the stage than center orchestra — less up-close, but the sound still carries well.
A noticeable side angle, but Imperial Theatre's more moderate size keeps the distance from the stage manageable.

vs.sum: The Imperial Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and solid sound quality, though some seats may miss minor stage action. While the ambiance is enhanced by its historic architectural design, comfort is average with decent legroom. Facilities are lacking, with long restroom lines being a common issue.

acc.note: 5 wheelchair locations in Orchestra. No steps from sidewalk. Infrared devices available.

vr.q: while it's a little one-note for 100 minutes, it is not a bad time
